summary:
In a space suit helmet, the CO2 that an astronaut breathes out can collect near the face. High CO2 causes headaches and slower thinking, and the astronaut may not notice it in time, most of all during hard work.

Nexxo is monitoring software for the CO2 sensor data of a helmet. It shows the CO2 value at four places in the helmet on a 3D model, with a color for each place: green, yellow, or red. It names the places where the CO2 rises, so the crew member sees the trend and not only the value. When a value passes the NASA limit, Nexxo sends an alert, in the page or on the full screen.

Nexxo does not take control and does not give orders. It turns sensor data into points of suggestion that can lead to action, and the astronaut decides what to do.

The limits come from NASA health documents: yellow starts at 2.3 mmHg, where station crews first report symptoms, and red starts above 3.0 mmHg, the NASA limit for the 1-hour average. In this prototype, the sensor values are a simulation that a presenter controls from a second page.

Our goal for the future is to improve the data that the suit collects and to give better points of suggestion. Two examples are a micro air jet at the places where the CO2 is high, and a local language model that explains each suggestion from the NASA protocols. The same idea could help crews on the Moon and on Mars, and firefighters, divers, and miners on Earth.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Nexxo has two pages. The helmet page is for the crew member. It shows a 3D helmet with four CO2 sensor places: the forehead, the mouth, the neck, and the back of the head. Each place has a value in mmHg and a color. A status line names the places where the CO2 rises. An alert shows in the page or covers the full screen, with the values and a suggested action.

The simulator page is for the presenter. It sets the sensor values, starts ready scenarios, and sends the alerts. A server sends each change to all open helmet pages at the same moment, so a full room sees the same data on their phones.

BENEFITS

One CO2 number for the whole suit can hide a pocket of high CO2 near the mouth. Nexxo shows where the CO2 is high, not only how high it is. It also shows the trend before the value passes the limit, so the crew member gets time to act.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want crew members to act before the symptoms start. Nexxo gives points of suggestion and the data behind them. It does not impose an action. The person always makes the decision. The same approach can work for cabins on the Moon and on Mars, and could help firefighters, divers, and miners on Earth.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

- TypeScript for all the code.

- React and Vite for the pages.

- three.js for the 3D helmet.

- Node.js and Express for the server, with server-sent events for the live data.

- Docker for the deploy.

- An AI coding assistant helped write the code.

The prototype uses no hardware. The sensor values are a simulation.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- The helmet is the real Apollo 11 helmet of Neil Armstrong, from the 3D scan of the Smithsonian. The CO2 shows as colored areas on it.

- The alert is a suggestion with a reason, not an alarm with an order.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Each limit has a NASA source. We say clearly that the sensor values are a simulation.

- The limits are those of a cabin, because we found no checked limit for the air inside a helmet.

- Existing sensors. NASA research already describes gas sensors for space suits and the problem of CO2 washout in the helmet. Nexxo adds the monitoring on top of that data.

- Access. The page works on a phone, in English and in Portuguese, and it uses shapes and text together with color. It could also work on a watch on an embedded device with a screen.

- The micro air jets and the local language model are ideas for the future. The prototype only simulates the first one.
